people.label: Ben R. Rich
people.sub: Director, Lockheed Advanced Development Projects (Skunk Works), 1975-1991
people.narrative: Rich is the single most-cited contractor figure in the custody allegation, and the most poorly sourced - which is exactly why he needs a disciplined entry. His documented record is not in dispute: he succeeded Kelly Johnson as head of Lockheed's Advanced Development Projects in 1975, ran the F-117 stealth fighter program to operational capability, held the deepest black-program access available to a private citizen in the United States, and retired in 1991. His 1994 memoir with Leo Janos, written after retirement and cleared for publication, is a first-person account of how unacknowledged special access programs were actually run at Burbank and Palmdale - the physical security, the compartmented staffing, the funding lines invisible to the aircraft's own users. That book is the primary document; it is also the reason his later remarks carry weight with researchers. The remarks themselves - the reported 1993 UCLA alumni-association talk in which he is said to have stated that 'we already have the means to travel among the stars, but these technologies are locked up in black projects,' and the reported private letters to model-maker John Andrews - survive only through secondhand recollection by attendees and correspondents. No recording, transcript, or letter facsimile has been produced in a verifiable archive. The board records the attribution as an attribution, not as a fact: what Rich unquestionably represents is that the man with the most complete inventory of American black aerospace in the twentieth century spent his last years being asked this question, and that Lockheed has never released his program records. He died of cancer on 5 January 1995.
affiliations: Lockheed Advanced Development Projects / Skunk Works, Director (1975-1991)
people.tierRationale: Tier B: his institutional position and access are documented at tier 1, but every specific UAP-custody utterance attributed to him rests on unrecorded secondhand testimony.

people.label: George Knapp
people.sub: Investigative journalist, KLAS-TV Las Vegas; sworn witness, 9 Sept 2025 House hearing
people.narrative: Knapp converted forty years of Nevada-desert sourcing into sworn congressional testimony on 9 September 2025, and in doing so put the contractor-custody allegation into the Congressional Record under his own name. Testifying before the House Oversight Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, he told the panel that Robert Bigelow and a colleague from the AAWSAP program 'met with and negotiated with senior executives at Lockheed Martin and hammered out a deal wherein Bigelow's company, BAASS, would receive a quantity of unusual material that had been stashed away and protected at a facility in California,' adding flatly: 'That material was not made here.' Asked directly by Rep. Tim Burchett which corporations hold the material, Knapp answered 'one of them is Lockheed,' declined to treat the company as villainous - 'they are doing what they were asked to do' - and offered the committee a list. Pressed by Rep. Nick Begich to name individual gatekeepers, he named Dr. James Ryder at Lockheed and, separately, Glenn Gaffney of CIA. He also placed on the record his interviews with Alfred O'Donnell, first general manager of EG&G in Nevada, and with Senators Harry Reid and Howard Cannon. Knapp's 1989 Bob Lazar reporting, which he re-affirmed in the same testimony, is the origin point of the modern S-4 reverse-engineering narrative. He is not a cleared insider and does not claim to be; his value is that he is a named journalist who has now sworn to his sourcing before Congress, converting decades of tier-3 anecdote into tier-2 record.

people.label: Luis Elizondo
people.sub: Former director, Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program (AATIP), OUSD(I)
people.narrative: Elizondo is the witness who put the contractor divestment attempt on the congressional record under oath. On 13 November 2024, before the House Oversight Committee, Rep. Eric Burlison asked him whether defense contractors possess technology. Elizondo answered that his predecessor program AAWSAP had tried to collect 'material of unknown origin,' that 'there was an aerospace contract company that requested to divest itself of the material... that was collected in the 1950s,' and that the transfer did not occur. Burlison then read to him the reporting of journalist Christopher Sharp describing a transfer between Lockheed Martin, Bigelow Aerospace and a CIA block; Elizondo replied 'What I can say is that it was blocked,' said he had later been told by contract personnel that the account was accurate, and explained the bureaucratic mechanism: the transfer required a memorandum from the Secretary of the Air Force that never came, after which he attempted to obtain one from Secretary of Defense James Mattis instead. Asked who possesses the material today, he refused to answer in open session. In the same hearing, Rep. Nancy Mace asked whether material is allocated to contractors by domain expertise - undersea propulsion to a General Dynamics, aerospace to Lockheed - and Elizondo replied 'Yes, ma'am, absolutely correct. Different contractors have different levels of expertise.' That exchange is the clearest description in any public record of how a distributed contractor custody architecture would function. Elizondo's statements are pre-publication-reviewed by DoD's Office of Prepublication and Security Review, a point he made in the hearing itself.

people.label: David Charles Grusch
people.sub: USAF Maj (ret.); NRO representative to the UAP Task Force 2019-2021; NGA GS-15
people.narrative: For this domain Grusch matters less for the crash-retrieval headline than for what he said about money. Under oath on 26 July 2023, Rep. Jared Moskowitz asked how an unreported program gets funded. Grusch answered: 'misappropriation of funds and self-fund.' Moskowitz pressed - are US corporations overcharging for technology they sell to the government, with the excess flowing to programs? Grusch: 'Correct, through something called IR&D.' Questioned by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez about notification requirements, he went further: 'IR&D is literally internal to the contractors. So, as long as it is money, either profits, private investment, et cetera, they do whatever they want.' In the same exchange he laid out the statutory architecture he says is being abused - 10 U.S.C. Sec. 119, the Secretary's authority to waive congressional reporting on special access programs, and the Gang of Eight notification that is supposed to backstop a waived unacknowledged SAP. Asked by AOC about contractor obligations to report UAP encounters, he answered: 'In terms of the contractors? Not that I am aware of.' Five months after that testimony, Congress wrote the IR&D loophole into law in reverse - NDAA FY2024 Sec. 1687(b) made UAP-related IR&D unallowable as an indirect expense unless disclosed to the defense and intelligence committees. Grusch named the mechanism in July; Congress legislated against that exact mechanism in December.

people.label: Robert T. Bigelow
people.sub: Founder, Bigelow Aerospace and BAASS; prime contractor for DIA's AAWSAP
people.narrative: Bigelow is the hinge between government money and private custody. His company Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies was the prime contractor on the Defense Intelligence Agency's AAWSAP award beginning in 2008, a special appropriation obtained through Senator Harry Reid. AARO's own Historical Record Report concedes the shape of what followed: the contractor team, with at least one supportive government program manager, conducted UAP and paranormal research at a property owned by the private sector organisation, and when DIA cancelled the effort its advocates proposed moving it to DHS as the KONA BLUE prospective special access program - a proposal whose explicit premise was that recovered technology already existed in hands that Congress could not reach. George Knapp told Congress under oath in September 2025 that Bigelow and an AAWSAP colleague negotiated directly with senior Lockheed Martin executives for a quantity of material held at a California facility, and Elizondo told Congress in 2024 that an aerospace contractor sought to divest 1950s-collected material and that the transfer was blocked. Bigelow built storage and handling capacity in Las Vegas on the expectation of receiving it. USAspending records roughly $30 million in federal prime contract obligations to Bigelow Aerospace LLC since FY2008 - the visible fraction of a much larger privately funded effort.
affiliations: Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies / BAASS (2008-2010s)

people.label: Alfred 'Al' O'Donnell
people.sub: Senior manager and first general manager, EG&G in Nevada; nuclear test firing engineer
people.narrative: O'Donnell is the highest-placed contractor executive ever alleged to have described recovered material directly to a journalist. He was an EG&G man from the Manhattan Project era forward - the firing-circuit engineer who triggered US atmospheric nuclear tests, and, per George Knapp, the first general manager of EG&G's Nevada operations, the company that ran the classified support infrastructure at the Nevada Test Site and the Groom Lake facility. Knapp interviewed him repeatedly beginning in the early 1990s and reported that O'Donnell told him 'they did have a flying saucer that had been recovered from New Mexico' and, separately, a 'live being': 'We didn't know what it was... To tell you the truth, we couldn't communicate with it. In the beginning, we didn't know what it was, we didn't know where it was from. And we didn't know what to do with it.' Knapp reported that O'Donnell compared the being's appearance to Ross Perot rather than to the conventional grey. With the blessing of EG&G co-founder Herbert Grier, Knapp arranged a meeting between O'Donnell and Senate Appropriations investigator Richard D'Amato - and O'Donnell told D'Amato nothing. Knapp says O'Donnell was subsequently warned off, but agreed to record a deathbed statement to be released after his death. No such recording has ever surfaced. O'Donnell is the test case for the entire contractor-custody thesis: a man with unimpeachable access, an account given privately and repeatedly, and a total absence of artifact.
people.tierRationale: Tier B: unimpeachable documented access to the relevant infrastructure; the custody account itself is single-source hearsay through one journalist, with the promised corroborating recording never produced.

people.label: Richard D'Amato
people.sub: Senate Appropriations Committee counsel/investigator for Sen. Robert C. Byrd, 1980s-1990s
people.narrative: D'Amato is the first documented attempt by the legislative branch to audit the contractor-custody allegation, and the template for every failure since. As a staffer to Senate Democratic Leader Robert C. Byrd - chairman of the Appropriations Committee - his portfolio covered the DoD budget and the National Foreign Intelligence Program, which meant special access program oversight. In the early 1990s a senior committee chairman asked him to conduct a preliminary inquiry into allegations of unidentified aerial crashes in 1940s New Mexico. He interviewed witnesses, visited the Nevada facility, and reported back that the basis for the allegations did not merit further Senate investigation. His public statement is terse and closed: 'I have no personal opinion on the matter and consider the inquiry to have been closed for over 20 years.' But according to George Knapp, D'Amato privately concluded it was 'entirely feasible, that this UFO cover-up exists within a private company' - naming Lockheed Martin, EG&G or Northrop Grumman as the kind of company he meant. The structural lesson is the one that recurs: an investigator with appropriations jurisdiction, sent to look, found that the relevant knowledge sat with a corporation rather than an agency, and that his subpoena power over an agency did not reach it. The witness he most needed - Al O'Donnell - said nothing when they met.

US-China Economic and Security Review Commission (2000s)

people.label: Robert M. Wood
people.sub: Physicist and R&D manager, McDonnell Douglas Astronautics, 1956-1993; co-founder, majesticdocuments.com
people.narrative: Wood is the documented instance of a prime contractor spending its own money to study the phenomenon - the IR&D pattern in its earliest and most benign form. A Cornell physics PhD, he spent his career at McDonnell Douglas Astronautics in Southern California on missile and space systems, and in the late 1960s ran a company-funded study of unidentified craft out of the Huntington Beach facility, on the reasoning that if the propulsion were real the company needed to know about it before a competitor did. That study is the direct ancestor of every later corporate 'internal interest' in the subject: not a government contract, not congressionally visible, funded from within the firm. After retiring in 1993 Wood turned to the documentary record, building with his son Ryan the majesticdocuments.com archive and applying forensic tests - typography, paper, security markings, terminology dating - to the Majestic-12 and related papers. That work is contested and the board treats the documents themselves as unresolved. Wood's value here is structural rather than evidentiary: he is a named senior engineer at a prime contractor who confirms from the inside that the primes looked, that they looked on their own dime, and that what they found was not reported anywhere Congress could see it.

people.label: Eric W. Davis
people.sub: Astrophysicist; EarthTech International, NIDS, AAWSAP DIRD author; Aerospace Corporation
people.narrative: Davis wrote the document that states the core allegation of this domain most precisely. The Wilson-Davis memorandum - notes attributed to Davis of a 16 October 2002 meeting with Vice Admiral Thomas Wilson, former Director of the Defense Intelligence Agency - describes Wilson being told that a recovered craft was held inside a special access program run by an aerospace contractor, and being refused access by the program's gatekeepers on the ground that he had no need to know. The memo's key sentence for this board is not about the craft at all: it is the reasoning that the material sat in corporate hands under proprietary protection, outside the chain Wilson could command. Davis has never authenticated the memo and Wilson has publicly denied the meeting; the pages surfaced from the files of Dr. Christopher 'Kit' Green. Independently of the memo, Davis is a documented participant in the funded record: an author of Defense Intelligence Reference Documents under DIA's AAWSAP contract, a NIDS scientist, and later an employee of the Aerospace Corporation, an FFRDC embedded in national security space. He briefed Senate Armed Services Committee staff on UAP matters in October 2019. AARO's Historical Record Report - without naming him - describes interviewees who alleged an organisation possessed off-world material in 2009-2010 and that a former senior CIA official quashed the proposal to remove it from the corporation.

entities.label: 10 U.S.C. Sec. 119 - Special access programs: congressional oversight

entities.desc: Section 119 of Title 10 is the statute the entire concealment argument runs through. Subsection (e) then supplies the escape: where the Secretary determines that disclosure would harm national security, the reporting obligation may be waived, and in that case the Secretary provides the information and the justification 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' rather than to the committees as a whole. lockheed-martin.desc: Longer note on the state of the Lockheed Martin allegation as of August 2026. Four independent strands converge on the company and none of them has produced a document. (1) Sworn testimony: George Knapp, 9 September 2025, on the BAASS negotiation for material at a California facility and on Lockheed as one of the corporate holders; Luis Elizondo, 13 November 2024, confirming that the divestment of 1950s-collected material was blocked. (2) Official record: AARO's Historical Record Report catalogues, without naming companies, an allegation that an organisation held twelve pre-1970 recovered craft with a CIA partnership ending in 1989, and a separate allegation that an organisation held off-world material in 2009-2010 whose return to government was quashed by a former senior CIA official. (3) Legislative record: the Senate voted for federal eminent domain over recovered technology 'controlled by private persons or entities' and the Senate Intelligence Committee voted to compel contractors to inventory 'all non-earth origin or exotic' material; both provisions were stripped in conference. (4) Investigative journalism: Christopher Sharp's reporting, read into a congressional hearing by Rep. Burlison and confirmed by the witness. What is absent is equally specific: no contract, no facility designation, no shipping document, no internal Lockheed record, no subpoena, no inspection, and no on-the-record response from the company to the sworn testimony naming it. AARO says the executives denied everything on the record; AARO does not say which executives, at which companies, or on what date, and describes no verification beyond the meeting itself.

ndaa-fy2024-sec1687.desc: The full operative text of Sec. 1687, Public Law 118-31, enacted 22 December 2023. Subsection (a): 'None of the funds authorized to be appropriated or otherwise made available by this Act may be obligated or expended in support of any activities involving unidentified anomalous phenomena protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations unless the Secretary of Defense has provided the details of the activity to the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership, including for any activities described in a report released by the All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office in fiscal year 2024.' Subsection (b): 'Consistent with Department of Defense Instruction Number 3204.01 (dated August 20, 2014, incorporating change 2, dated July 9, 2020; relating to Department policy for oversight of independent research and development), independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction, unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership.' Subsection (c) defines the appropriate committees as the congressional defense committees plus both intelligence committees, and congressional leadership as the four party leaders. Section 7343 imposes the identical structure on intelligence appropriations through the Director of National Intelligence. Neither provision has produced any publicly reported disclosure.

iaa-fy2024-sec1104.desc: The contractor provisions of S. 2103 Sec. 1104 as reported by the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence on 22 June 2023, none of which became law. Subsection (c) lists the activities to be defunded absent disclosure: '(A) Recruiting, employing, training, equipping, and operations of, and providing security for, government or contractor personnel with a primary, secondary, or contingency mission of capturing, recovering, and securing unidentified anomalous phenomena craft or pieces and components of such craft. (B) Analyzing such craft or pieces or components thereof, including for the purpose of determining properties, material composition, method of manufacture, origin, characteristics, usage and application, performance, operational modalities, or reverse engineering of such craft or component technology. (C) Managing and providing security for protecting activities and information relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena from disclosure or compromise. (D) Actions relating to reverse engineering or replicating unidentified anomalous phenomena technology or performance... (E) The development of propulsion technology, or aerospace craft that uses propulsion technology, systems, or subsystems, that is based on or derived from or inspired by inspection, analysis, or reverse engineering of recovered unidentified anomalous phenomena craft or materials. (F) Any aerospace craft that uses propulsion technology other than chemical propellants, solar power, or electric ion thrust.' Subsection (d) requires notification to the DNI within 60 days and production within 180 days, including 'a comprehensive list of all non-earth origin or exotic unidentified anomalous phenomena material.' Subsection (e) grants immunity from criminal and civil action for compliance. Subsection (f) carries the IR&D restriction. A Senate committee does not draft six categories of activity in that detail about a null set.

aaro-historical-record-vol1.desc: Additional passages from AARO Volume I that bear directly on contractor custody. On the companies: 'Named Companies Allegedly Experimenting on Alien Technology: AARO has found no evidence that U.S. companies ever possessed off-world technology. The executives, scientists, and chief technology officers of the companies named by interviewees met with the Director of AARO and denied on the record that they have ever recovered, possessed, or engaged in reverse-engineering of extraterrestrial technology.' On the twelve-craft allegation: 'An AARO interviewee claimed in a thirdhand account that an organization was in possession of 12 spacecraft recovered from different crash events prior to 1970. Some of the craft allegedly were intact. The interviewee also stated that the CIA had a partnership with the company that ended in 1989 and wanted all material returned to the CIA.' On the 2009-2010 material: 'An interviewee claimed that an organization was in possession of off-world material in 2009 and 2010. A separate interviewee stated they participated in negotiations to return the material to the USG. The same interviewee stated that a former named senior CIA official quashed the proposal to remove the material from the corporation.' On the proprietary mechanism: a former senior US military officer 'gave a detailed description of a craft floating in a building. The officer told the interviewee that approximately 150 individuals were working on the program and that the program was kept outside of government so the technology could remain proprietary.' On future work: 'Engage with commercial entities on named companies alleged to have worked with the USG on UAP recovery and alleged exploitation of UAP technology.' No subsequent AARO publication reports the result of that engagement.

gaps: No contractor has ever been subpoenaed. Across three House hearings (2023, 2024, 2025) at which Lockheed Martin was named on the record, no company representative was called, no document production was compelled, and no committee has reported requesting one.

George Knapp offered the House a list of the contractors holding material on 9 September 2025 ('There is a list I can give you, Congressman'). No list has been published and no committee has reported receiving it. This is the single highest-value outstanding item in the domain.

Dr. James Ryder's position, dates and portfolio at Lockheed Martin are unverified. He was named once, under oath, and neither he nor the company has publicly responded. A corporate org-chart or press record would move this from tier 2 to tier 1 or kill it.
The 'facility in California' where the material was allegedly held has never been named by any witness. Candidate sites in Lockheed's California footprint are inference only.

AARO does not name the companies whose executives denied the allegations, does not date the meetings, and does not describe any inspection, audit or document review beyond the meetings. A FOIA for the AARO memoranda for record of those corporate meetings has not been reported.

No public accounting exists of any disclosure made under NDAA FY2024 Sec. 1687(a) or (b), or under Sec. 7343. If no disclosure was ever made, either no such activity exists or the statute is being ignored - and no committee has said which.

Contractor IR&D project summaries are submitted to the Defense Innovation Marketplace and reviewed by contracting officers and DCAA for cost allowability. Those submissions are a records set that exists, is government-held, and has never been searched for UAP-related entries.

No McDonnell Douglas or Boeing internal record of Robert Wood's late-1960s Huntington Beach study has been released or requested, despite Boeing having inherited the organisation and its files in 1997.
The alleged Alfred O'Donnell deathbed recording has never surfaced. Its existence rests entirely on Knapp's account and on a secondhand confirmation from O'Donnell's son.

The provenance chain of the Wilson-Davis memorandum between the alleged October 2002 meeting and its 2019 public circulation from Kit Green's holdings is undocumented. Davis has never authenticated it; Wilson has denied the meeting.

Radiance Technologies recurs in UAP-adjacent reporting as an employer of personnel who moved between government UAP work and industry, but no primary personnel record has been located. This entry is deliberately thin rather than padded.

The Pax River storage claim rests on unnamed sources plus Elizondo's written congressional testimony. The written testimony itself should be pulled from the House document repository and quoted directly.

The Ben Rich quotations - the 1993 UCLA remark and the John Andrews letters - have no archival primary source. A recording, transcript, contemporaneous note or letter facsimile would be the single most valuable artifact recoverable in this domain, and thirty years of searching has not produced one.
The charter of the 2026 interagency UAP Governance Board has been quoted only in its mission paragraph. Whether it contains any provision reaching contractor-held material or records is unknown.

No UAP-labelled contract action appears anywhere in USAspending or FPDS. Either the work is entirely classified out of the public procurement record, is funded through IR&D and overhead as Grusch alleged, or does not exist.
